title: Crypto misuse: RSA verify wc_RsaSSL_Verify return-value check uses wrong convention
description: In wolfssl_rsa_verify (wolfssl_rsa.c), wc_RsaSSL_Verify returns positive on success (length of recovered message), or a wolfCrypt negative error code on failure. The check 'if (ret > 0)' is therefore correct for the success path. However, if wc_RsaSSL_Verify returns exactly 0 (e.g. zero-length recovered message — theoretically impossible for PKCS#1 v1.5 but not impossible for all RSA modes), the else branch calls wolfssl_rsa_xlat_err(0). That function's switch statement has no case for 0, so it falls through to 'default: return -EIO' — logging a spurious pr_err and returning -EIO rather than -EBADMSG. The actual security consequence is minor (verify fails with wrong errno), but the return-value convention comment in the CLAUDE.md says wolfCrypt returns 0 for success and must be checked with \!= 0, while wc_RsaSSL_Verify actually uses a different convention (positive = bytes written). This is a documentation/convention inconsistency that makes the code harder to audit. The check should use explicit: if (ret > 0) success; if (ret == 0) unexpected zero-length (treat as -EBADMSG); if (ret < 0) wolfCrypt error. Priority downgraded: no actual security bypass exists because xlat_err(0) returns -EIO not 0.
